explanations.explanation: Yep, the mouth, friend. David says, "I will watch my ways so that I will not sin with my tongue; I will guard my mouth with a muzzle…" (Psalm 39:1). He's not guarding his words because he's shy. He says it's so he won't sin with his tongue. Honestly, we've all had a moment where a muzzle would've saved us a whole conversation.

Not the eyes, friend. David never mentions them here. He says he will watch his ways "so that I will not sin with my tongue" (Psalm 39:1). His eyes are free to roam. It's his mouth that's getting locked up.

Close, because the heart does show up in this psalm, but not here. In verse 1, David says, "I will guard my mouth with a muzzle…" (Psalm 39:1). The heart gets its moment in verse 3, and it's a hot one. For now, the guard is on the mouth.

Careful, friend, that one's a trap. David says, "I was speechless and still; I remained silent, even from speaking good…" (Psalm 39:2). So the muzzle held back the good words too. Nothing came out at all.

That's right, baker. The text says David "remained silent, even from speaking good" (Psalm 39:2). The muzzle didn't sort his words into good and bad. It just shut the whole shop. And the verse adds that his sorrow was stirred.

That's it, baker. David says, "My heart grew hot within me; as I mused, the fire burned." (Psalm 39:3). He kept it all in, and the inside didn't stay quiet. I think anybody who's ever held in a big feeling knows that heat. Then he finally speaks.

You'd think all that silence would bring some calm, friend. But David says the opposite: "My heart grew hot within me; as I mused, the fire burned." (Psalm 39:3). Quiet on the outside, a fire on the inside. That's why he finally speaks.
No numbness here, friend. David feels all of it. He says, "My heart grew hot within me…" (Psalm 39:3). A fire burning is the opposite of numb. I think he felt every degree of it.

explanations.answer: His end and the measure of his days
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. David prays, "Show me, O LORD, my end and the measure of my days. Let me know how fleeting my life is." (Psalm 39:4). After all that silence, you might expect a complaint about the wicked. Instead he asks about how short life is. That's a surprise, and I like it.

explanations.answer: The plans the wicked have against him
explanations.explanation: The wicked do show up in verse 1, friend, but David doesn't ask about their plans. When he finally speaks, he says, "Show me, O LORD, my end and the measure of my days." (Psalm 39:4). His question turns toward his own days. That's the first thing out of his mouth.

explanations.answer: The reason his sorrow got stirred up
explanations.explanation: It's a fair guess, since the sorrow was stirred in verse 2. But David doesn't ask for a reason. He asks, "Show me, O LORD, my end and the measure of my days." (Psalm 39:4). The text doesn't tell us why he went there, so I won't guess either.

Short is right, baker. David says, "You, indeed, have made my days as handbreadths…" (Psalm 39:5). A handbreadth is about the width of your hand, and that's a tiny measure for a whole life. He even asked to know "how fleeting my life is" (Psalm 39:4). Hold up your hand and look at it for a second.
If only, friend! But David says the opposite. He calls his days "handbreadths" (Psalm 39:5), which is about the width of your hand. That's a very small measure. Nobody calls a handbreadth long.
Safe isn't the word here, friend. The handbreadth is about size, not safety. David says, "You, indeed, have made my days as handbreadths…" (Psalm 39:5). A hand is small, so his days are short.

That's it, baker. David says every man "bustles in vain" and "heaps up riches not knowing who will haul them away." (Psalm 39:6). All that rushing around, and he doesn't even know who ends up with the pile. It's like a man who packs a cookie box for months and has no idea whose table it lands on.

Nope, friend. David doesn't say the bustling wins anything from the LORD. He says every man "bustles in vain" (Psalm 39:6). In vain means it doesn't get you anywhere. The riches get hauled away by someone he can't even name.

That's a different worry, friend. Here David isn't talking about the wicked at all. He says every man "bustles in vain; he heaps up riches not knowing who will haul them away." (Psalm 39:6). It's about the bustling coming to nothing.

True, baker! David asks, "And now, O Lord, for what do I wait?" and then answers himself right away: "My hope is in You." (Psalm 39:7). After talking about breath and phantoms, he lands on the one place he puts his hope. I think that's the turn of the whole psalm.

Not false, friend. David asks the question and then answers it in the same breath: "My hope is in You." (Psalm 39:7). He doesn't leave the question hanging. After all that talk of fleeting days, his hope has a place to land.

Yes, baker. David says, "I have become mute; I do not open my mouth because of what You have done." (Psalm 39:9). He's speaking to the Lord, and he points to what the Lord has done. The fools and the friends aren't the reason here.

The fools do get a mention, friend, back in verse 8, where David asks not to be their reproach. But in verse 9 he says, "I do not open my mouth because of what You have done." (Psalm 39:9). The "You" is the Lord. The fools aren't the reason for the silence.

Friends don't appear in this part at all, baker. David says, "I have become mute; I do not open my mouth because of what You have done." (Psalm 39:9). He's talking straight to the Lord. No friends in the room.

Not quite, friend. David says the Lord corrects a man for his iniquity, "consuming like a moth what he holds dear" (Psalm 39:11). A moth eats away at what's in the closet. So what he holds dear does not stay safe.

Right, baker. The verse says the Lord is "consuming like a moth what he holds dear; surely each man is but a vapor." (Psalm 39:11). A moth doesn't ask permission, it just eats the sweater. So what a man holds dear isn't safe.

That's right, baker. David says, "For I am a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers." (Psalm 39:12). He's not the first one to feel like a visitor here. Those who came before him did too.

Other way around, friend. David looks back, not forward. He says, "For I am a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers." (Psalm 39:12). It's his fathers who stood where he's standing.

Good thought, but friends aren't in this line. David says, "For I am a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers." (Psalm 39:12). It's his fathers he names. He's got a long line behind him.

explanations.answer: Turn His gaze away from him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. David prays, "Turn Your gaze away from me, that I may again be cheered before I depart and am no more." (Psalm 39:13). It's a heavy way to end a psalm, and I think this one hurts. He asks to be cheered again before his days are done.

You'd think so, friend, but that's not the ask. David says, "Turn Your gaze away from me, that I may again be cheered before I depart and am no more." (Psalm 39:13). He's not asking for more years. He's asking to be cheered again before he goes.

No enemies in this last line, friend. David asks, "Turn Your gaze away from me, that I may again be cheered before I depart and am no more." (Psalm 39:13). The wicked were in verse 1, but the psalm ends on his own days and his own cheer.
